source.title: Compressed Computation under $L^4$ Loss is likely Computation in Superposition
source.citation: Francisco Ferreira da Silva et al., 2026
source.authors: Francisco Ferreira da Silva; S. Heimersheim

record.file_problem: The supplied text is cut off during Appendix C, after the edge-swap procedure begins.
record.tranche_reason: Tests computation in superposition in a trained toy network, an adjacent setting to the claim’s neuron-polysemanticity mechanism; it does not study neuron meanings in image or language models.
record.gate_note: The paper’s own results concern computation of 100 sparse-input ReLUs with 50 hidden neurons, not whether neurons in ordinary trained networks have coherent or mixed semantic meanings. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows. The measured sparse code and per-feature outcomes bear on V3’s packed-features mechanism only in this computation setting.
record.test_reason: In a trained toy network with 100 sparse features and 50 neurons, each neuron joins about 11 feature codewords. This shows neurons shared across unrelated features because features outnumber neurons, which bears on V3. The setting is computation, not representation, in superposition, and the packing appears only under loss exponents above 2.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, but the authors hedge: L4 training 'likely' elicits computation in superposition. The trained network uses sparse binary codewords over neurons, read out by a near-pseudoinverse decoder. Under L2 it finds the naive solution. The work resembles Hänni et al.'s random sparse codes, though the match is suggestive rather than exact.
record.recipe_differences: Trains a synthetic one-hidden-layer ReLU network on sparse featurewise ReLU regression under a sweep of loss exponents, then reverse-engineers its codewords and decoder; it does not use the original sources’ neuron-visualization or activation-function methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome changes with loss exponent: L2 gives the naive solution while all tested exponents above 2 give an even per-feature error spread. The weaker embedding-dimension-50 setting has a higher coefficient of variation than the dimension-1000 setting.
record.problems: Toy network and synthetic sparse-input task; the study does not measure neuron semantic meanings in ordinary vision or language models. The supplied text is cut off during Appendix C, and the larger-model-size check reports only the loss-spread statistic rather than the full binary-code mechanism.
record.rows_left_out: No other distinct numeric outcomes bearing on V3 were omitted from the supplied text. Some synthetic-code sweep values are shown only in Figure 7 and are not individually stated in the text; they are not entered as separate rows.

untested.parts: Representational superposition in ordinary trained vision or language networks, and whether it explains semantically mixed neuron responses.
The loss exponent changes whether packing occurs, but the share of polysemantic neurons under L2 is not measured. No activation-function or architecture comparison is made.
Untested: the sufficient-capacity regime is not studied.
Untested: canonical neurons are not reinterpreted.
Untested beyond a fixed 0.05 on-code threshold.

missing.what: Embedded-model codeword length 5–7 and swap-test pass rate 99.9%, showing neuron sharing replicates with the embedding.
Neurons in more codewords have lower on-code values (r ≈ −0.82), indicating load-balancing of shared neurons.

record.verdict_notes: Polysemanticity here means synthetic features sharing neurons in a computation task. It is not semantic mixing in real models. Rows r7–r11 describe the authors' reconstruction and designed codes and were unlinked. The text is truncated in Appendix C.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier neurons or image inputs are studied.
No transformer language models, MLP neurons, tokens, or contexts are studied.

Tests packing computations for sparse input features in a toy network, not whether polysemantic neurons arise from representational superposition in ordinary trained networks or whether that mechanism explains semantic neuron responses.
Does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.

Varies the loss exponent for computation in a toy ReLU network, but does not measure the share of polysemantic neurons or compare SoLU, modern convnets, or performance costs of reducing neuron polysemanticity.
Does not reinterpret semantic mixtures in canonical neurons or test whether they share one feature.
Does not vary the activation-range or explanation-scoring method for identifying polysemantic neurons.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer ReLU network trained under L2 loss
rows.operation_detail: Trained on the sparse-feature ReLU task under L2 loss; measured coefficient of variation of per-feature MSE.
rows.measure: Coefficient of variation of per-feature MSE across 100 features
rows.uncertainty: Across seeds, coefficient of variation varies by at most 0.003 throughout the exponent sweep.
rows.note: The paper characterizes this as the naive solution: half the features are learned and the rest largely ignored.
rows.check: Under L2 the network ignores half the features rather than packing them, despite the same 2:1 feature-to-neuron ratio. Capacity pressure alone does not produce superposition here.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4.1, Figure 2: L2 gives naive solution, CV 0.999

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer ReLU network trained under L4 loss
rows.operation_detail: Trained on the sparse-feature ReLU task under L4 loss; measured coefficient of variation of per-feature MSE.
rows.measure: Coefficient of variation of per-feature MSE across 100 features
rows.value: 0.031 in the embedded-model comparison; the main-text sweep reports 0.028–0.046 across exponents above 2.
rows.uncertainty: Across seeds, coefficient of variation varies by at most 0.003 throughout the exponent sweep.
rows.note: The error is spread relatively evenly across features; the paper interprets this as evidence of computation in superposition.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer ReLU networks trained with loss exponents above 2
rows.operation_detail: Swept the training loss exponent and measured per-feature error spread.
rows.measure: Coefficient of variation of per-feature MSE across 100 features
rows.value: Between 0.028 and 0.046 for every tested exponent above 2
rows.uncertainty: Across seeds, coefficient of variation varies by at most 0.003 throughout.
rows.note: The paper says every tested exponent above 2 gives a superposition-like solution; L4 is described as representative, not unique.

rows.subject: no-superposition baselines: naive and emulate-bias solutions
rows.size_stated: 100 input/output features; 50 hidden neurons for trained-network comparison
rows.operation_detail: Compared L4 loss of the no-superposition baselines with the trained L4 solution.
rows.measure: L4 loss relative to the trained L4 network
rows.value: Emulate-bias baseline is about 7% lower loss than naive, but remains about 26× the L4 solution; naive baseline is about 28× the L4 solution.
rows.note: The paper presents both as no-superposition baselines.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer ReLU network trained under L4 loss
rows.operation_detail: Classified encoder entries as on-code or off-code and counted the codeword memberships.
rows.measure: Codeword length per feature and number of codewords per neuron
rows.value: Each feature uses 5–7 neurons (mean 5.5); each neuron participates in 10–12 codewords (mean 10.9).
rows.note: The reported pattern is close to biregular, with neuron use spread relatively evenly.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer ReLU network trained under L4 loss

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer ReLU network trained under L4 loss
rows.operation_detail: Compared the trained decoder with a scaled pseudoinverse of the encoder.
rows.measure: Frobenius cosine between trained decoder and scaled encoder pseudoinverse
rows.note: The paper describes the decoder as a near-pseudoinverse readout of the codewords.
rows.check: Decoder–pseudoinverse similarity describes the readout mechanism, not whether neurons are shared across features.

rows.subject: single-hidden-layer ReLU network with its trained encoder and a post-hoc pseudoinverse decoder
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the trained decoder with a scaled pseudoinverse of the encoder.

conditions.value: scaled encoder pseudoinverse, substituted post hoc

rows.measure: L4 loss relative to the trained network

rows.check: A post-hoc decoder replacement compared against the study's own trained network. It measures fidelity of the description, not polysemanticity.

rows.subject: three-scalar network using the trained network’s codewords
rows.stage_stated: constructed from a trained network’s codewords
rows.operation_detail: Set encoder entries using on-code, off-code, and decoder-scale scalars; used a scaled pseudoinverse decoder.
rows.measure: L4 loss relative to the trained network
rows.note: The compact description recovers most, but not all, of the trained network’s performance.
rows.check: The three-scalar ansatz is the study's own reconstruction, compared against the trained net. It is not a measure of superposition arising.

rows.subject: hand-designed biregular binary-code network
rows.operation_detail: Used an overlap-minimized biregular K = 5 code in the three-scalar ansatz with a pseudoinverse decoder.
rows.measure: L4 loss relative to the trained network
rows.uncertainty: Five seeds; error bars are standard deviations.
rows.note: This is the best reported designed code; no synthetic code beats the trained network.
rows.check: A hand-designed network, constructed rather than trained; it is the study's method compared with the trained network.

rows.subject: hand-designed binary-code networks
rows.operation_detail: Compared random and biregular codes with and without overlap-minimizing edge swaps in the three-scalar ansatz.

conditions.value: sweep over K; exact values not stated for all conditions

rows.measure: L4 loss relative to the trained network
rows.value: Without overlap minimization both families are 1.7–2.0×; with overlap minimization, best designed code is about 1.12×.
rows.uncertainty: Five seeds; error bars are standard deviations.
rows.note: Overlap reduction improves the designed-code results; the supplied text does not give every plotted value.
rows.check: Hand-designed codes; method comparison rather than a result on the claim.
